Choice Restriction.short_definition: Closing off or hiding realistic alternatives one by one, so that a single outcome ends up looking like the only sensible choice.
Choice Restriction.core_meaning: Closing off or hiding realistic alternatives one by one, so that a single outcome ends up looking like the only sensible choice.
Choice Restriction.expanded_definition: Choice restriction narrows what you can realistically do, through money, access, information or the way options are described, until one outcome is left standing. Choice Architecture Manipulation is simply another name for this: some readers notice the closed doors, others notice how the menu was laid out. No demand is ever made, so there is nothing to refuse. One short list of options means little. The pattern is that the list keeps shrinking in the same direction.
Choice Restriction.plain_language_summary: Your options get closed off or made to look unworkable one at a time, until the choice someone else would prefer is the only one that seems left.
Choice Restriction.why_this_matters: No demand is made, so there is nothing to push back on. By the time you notice, you may have agreed to something you never really picked, with no single moment to point to when you ask how you got here.
what_it_is: Alternatives removed in practice: an account closed, a ride not offered, a form never handed over, a deadline you were not told about.
Alternatives made to sound unworkable by the way they are described, so one choice sounds sensible and the rest sound foolish or costly.
The preferred option made easiest, as the default, the one already filled in, scheduled or paid for.
Information held back or sorted so you cannot compare, such as quotes you never see.
Found in households, workplaces, sales settings, families and care arrangements, wherever one person handles the money, paperwork, schedule or information.
what_it_sounds_like: You don't really have a choice here.
You could do the second one, but you'd lose your whole routine and it never works out. The first is simple.
I already booked the one that works. You just need to sign.
There's no point looking at other places. I called around and they're all full.
The third option? Honestly, nobody sensible picks that.
I have the forms for this one ready. The others take weeks of paperwork.
Only one form is on the table, already filled in, and the other routes are never mentioned.
Looking back, every path I was offered ended in the same place.
what_it_is_not: Options are often truly limited by outside constraints nobody arranged, such as a tight budget, a small town or a full calendar.
Honest advice about which of several real options is best, with the others left available to you.
A sensible default set for practical reasons, like a standard meeting time you can change.
A person who only knows a few options, shares them, and welcomes the others when you find them.
A menu of fixed packages shown openly with prices side by side.
Circumstances narrowing over time, as a lease ends or a workplace closes, with nobody steering.
this_may_be_it_when: Each time you name another possibility there is a reason it will not work, and the reasons all point the same way.
The person describing the options also controls the money, paperwork, schedule or information you would need to check them.
Options you would normally consider have disappeared without any conversation about removing them.
Looking into an alternative on your own is met with irritation, or you find it was more open than you were told.
The outcome that is left happens to suit the person doing the narrowing.
this_may_not_be_it_when: You can look up alternatives yourself and the other person is happy for you to do it.
The options that are gone were closed by a landlord, bank, rule or deadline that neither of you controls.
When you pick the option they like less, they help you carry it out.
They set out the trade-offs for every option, including the ones they like least.
Checking shows the other options really are unworkable for reasons you can verify.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People with a strong view often describe the options they dislike less kindly, without noticing they are doing it.
Someone short of time may offer one workable plan instead of a full menu, to save effort.
Real costs such as price, distance or waiting lists make some options unattractive for anyone.
common_false_positives: A tutor or gym that offers three fixed packages and shows the prices openly.
A friend helping with a move who says the only day they can come is Saturday.
A doctor who recommends one treatment strongly while telling you the others exist and what they involve.
discernment_questions: If I looked for another option on my own, what would I find, and who told me it was not possible?
Who gains from the option that is left?
Do the reasons for ruling out each alternative come from the person, or from something I can check?
Can I get my own quotes, copies of paperwork or advice from someone else without trouble?
Would a neutral person who saw all the same facts name the same single option?
less_concerning_if: The limits come from a source you can check, such as a published rule or price list.
You can freely ask others for advice and the answer is not met with displeasure.
When you do pick differently, nothing about your life gets harder.
more_concerning_if: The person narrowing your options also controls your money, housing, documents or contact with other people.
Looking for alternatives is discouraged, or you are told the people who might offer them cannot be trusted.
Choosing a different option brings a loss, such as support being withdrawn or a long punishing silence.
pattern_over_time_signs: The things you feel free to do on your own shrink, one exception at a time.
You stop looking for alternatives because past searches always came to nothing.
Decisions that used to be yours, such as where to live, work or spend, are now described as obvious.
You struggle to name one thing you chose that went against what the other person wanted.
Choice Restriction.repair_check: Repair here is practical: the closed doors reopen. The missing options get named, information you were not given is shared openly, and a choice that goes against their preference is accepted without a penalty. A warm apology while the same short menu stays in place changes little.
Choice Restriction.boundary_respect_check: Watch what happens to the second option once you ask about it. Does it get a fair description with its real costs, or one more reason it will not work? And if you choose it, does your ordinary day stay as it was?
Choice Restriction.psychological_mechanism: We usually choose from what is in front of us and seldom go looking for what is missing. When alternatives are removed or described as costly, the remaining option may read as your own conclusion, because no one ever asked you for anything. Objecting afterwards is hard, since you can recall agreeing but not choosing.
Choice Restriction.possible_impact_on_receiver: Many report a puzzled sense of having said yes to something they never wanted, and trouble explaining how it happened. Some feel foolish for not looking harder. Others say they started to distrust their own judgement, or stopped making plans because the plans never seemed to survive the facts they were handed.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the missing options by name: 'Could we write down every way this could go, including the ones you think are unlikely, before we settle on one?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep the decision open: 'I'm not ready to treat that as the only option. I'd like to look into one or two others myself before I answer.'
response_options.disengagement: Without announcing anything, keep a private note of which options disappeared, when, and who said so, somewhere only you can reach. Weigh big decisions about housing or money quietly, with an advocate.
response_options.support_seeking: Describe the situation to someone outside it, or to an advocate, and ask them to list the options they see. If their list is longer than yours, that is useful information.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask in writing which alternatives were considered and who ruled them out. If the answer is vague, ask a union representative, HR or an ombuds office to look at it.

Choice Restriction.boundary_script: "I'd like to see all the options laid out side by side, including the ones that look unlikely. Could we list what each one involves, and then I'll take it from there?"
Choice Restriction.safety_note: The picture changes when the closed options involve money, housing, documents, medical care or contact with other people, and the person closing them is the one who controls those things. Watch for being told you could not manage elsewhere, or being unable to see accounts or papers. Speak with a domestic abuse advocate or legal aid service before changing anything, and plan any change privately.
misuse_warning: Calling it whenever an option you liked becomes unavailable can turn landlords, budgets and bad luck into someone's strategy. Check first whether the limit is real and can be verified.
Telling someone who gave you honest, strongly worded advice that they restricted your choices can turn a plain disagreement into a charge.
Choice Restriction.how_to_distinguish_from_related: False Dilemma is a statement, usually spoken, that there are only two options when more exist, so it can be challenged on the spot. Choice restriction often has no statement at all; the other options are closed in practice or described out of reach. Ultimatums attach a threatened loss to a forced either-or, while no threat is needed here. Resource Sabotage removes what you need to succeed, then blames you for the result, while this removes the alternatives to one outcome.

Foot-in-the-Door.short_definition: Winning a small yes first, then using it to secure a larger one, so each agreement makes the next harder to refuse.
Foot-in-the-Door.core_meaning: Winning a small yes first, then using it to secure a larger one, so each agreement makes the next harder to refuse.
Foot-in-the-Door.expanded_definition: Foot-in-the-door begins with something easy to agree to, then follows with something bigger that leans on the first yes. It can be one jump or a ladder of many small steps. Graduated Compliance and Commitment Traps are other names for exactly this: one stresses the small steps, the other the obligation piled up by the end. One favour followed by a bigger one means little, since requests grow in ordinary friendships. The pattern is that the earlier yes is cited as the reason for the next.
Foot-in-the-Door.plain_language_summary: You agree to something small. Then a bigger ask arrives, and your first yes is used as a reason you should not say no to this one.
Foot-in-the-Door.why_this_matters: The larger request is judged against what you already agreed to, not on its own terms. You can end up carrying an obligation you never chose at any single moment, and refusing starts to feel like going back on your word.
what_it_is: A small, easy request that gets a yes, followed by a larger request on the same theme.
Either a single jump (a quick favour, then a big one) or a ladder of many steps, each barely bigger than the last.
Draws on the common habit of staying consistent with what we have already said and done.
Appears in sales, fundraising, volunteering, workplaces and close relationships, for example a free sample followed by a plea to buy.
Leaves a final obligation that nobody named at the start and that you never agreed to as a whole.
what_it_sounds_like: Could you just look over this one page? It'll take two minutes.
You already helped with the first part, so it makes sense for you to finish it.
You said yes to the trial, so signing the full contract is really just the next step.
It's only a small change from what we did last time.
Since you covered one shift, could you take the whole weekend?
We've come this far together. You wouldn't back out now.
A free gift is handed over, and the request for a donation that follows mentions the gift.
what_it_is_not: Small favours that grow into larger ones naturally and mutually, with real consent at each stage, are how most relationships work.
Someone who asks for something small, gets it, and only later finds they need something bigger, with no sequence in mind.
A large request that stands on its own merits whatever came before it.
A trial whose price and cancellation terms were shown clearly before you began.
A role that grows as trust is earned, with each increase named out loud and agreed.
Volunteering for more because you enjoy the work.
this_may_be_it_when: The bigger request cites your earlier yes as its main reason.
The first request was unusually small or easy compared with what followed.
Looking back, you could not have named the full scope at the beginning, because it was never said.
Trying to scale back is described as going back on your word.
Each step is called basically the same as the last, though the total is far larger.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The bigger ask would sound reasonable if it came cold, and you could say no to it easily.
Both of you would describe the current arrangement in the same terms.
Saying no to a stage leaves your earlier help appreciated, not cancelled.
The person told you early what the whole task might involve.
The increases were discussed and agreed at each stage.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Many tasks show their real size only once begun, and a person may honestly ask for more after seeing it.
People naturally ask those who have helped before, because they know them to be willing.
Trust grows in steps, and a bigger request can be a sign of closeness.
common_false_positives: A neighbour who borrows a ladder, then asks to borrow the car later in the month, and accepts a no.
A volunteer coordinator who asks someone who enjoyed one event to help with the next.
A clearly priced trial whose terms were on screen before you started.
discernment_questions: If the bigger request had come first, with no earlier yes, would I agree to it?
Can I name what was said about the full scope at the start?
Is my earlier agreement being used as the reason, in place of a reason about the request itself?
Can I scale back without hearing that I am going back on my word?
Are the steps growing faster than the relationship, or the pay, can carry?
less_concerning_if: The bigger ask is made openly with its full size stated, and a no is received calmly.
The earlier yes is mentioned as history, not used as a lever.
You feel free to return to an earlier level of involvement.
more_concerning_if: Your past yeses are tallied up whenever you hesitate.
The steps keep growing and there is never a point at which the total is stated.
Stepping back costs something concrete, such as your standing in the group or at work.
pattern_over_time_signs: You find yourself doing things you would have refused if asked outright, with no single moment you can point to.
Requests tend to arrive right after you say yes to something.
You start refusing small things early, to avoid where they might lead.
Reminders of what you already did come up whenever you hesitate.
Foot-in-the-Door.repair_check: Repair means the whole size of the ask is said out loud, and you get a real chance to start again from where you want to stand. Being thanked for earlier help while the extra load stays exactly where it was is appreciation, not repair.
Foot-in-the-Door.boundary_respect_check: Notice whether your earlier yes is thanked or tallied. When a boundary is respected, the first favour stays a gift. When it is not, the favour turns into a debt that gets raised each time you hesitate.
Foot-in-the-Door.psychological_mechanism: Most of us like to act in line with what we have said and done before, and a first yes can make a later request seem a continuation of who we are. Small steps keep the cost of each yes low, so no single step prompts a pause. The total shows itself only when you compare the start with where you stand now.
Foot-in-the-Door.possible_impact_on_receiver: A creeping sense of being stuck in something never signed up for is common, along with a hard time saying when it began. Some feel embarrassed at having said yes so often. Others begin refusing small, harmless requests early to avoid where they might lead, which can strain ordinary generosity.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for the whole picture: 'Before I say yes to this part, what else would come next? I'd like to know the full size of it.'
response_options.firm_boundary: Separate the steps: 'I agreed to the first part. This is a new request, and I'm deciding it on its own.'
response_options.disengagement: Finish the part you agreed to, and decline to start the next stage until it is written down.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend the whole sequence in order and ask whether they would have agreed to the last step if it had come first.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask for new duties to be added to your role description or confirmed by email, with any change in pay or hours, before you take them on.

Foot-in-the-Door.boundary_script: "I was glad to do the first part, and I'm treating this as a new request. Can you tell me what the whole thing involves? I'll decide about this part once I can see that."
Foot-in-the-Door.safety_note: By itself this is a pressure pattern, not a danger sign. It changes when the steps start to involve money, signing legal papers, sexual activity or secrecy, or when stopping brings threats. Before agreeing to anything with legal or financial weight, show the papers to someone outside the situation, such as a legal aid service or a trusted adviser.
misuse_warning: A follow-up request after a favour is not automatically a trap. Applying the label to ordinary friends can make it hard to ask for or give help at all.
Naming a sequence tells you what happened, not what anyone planned. Treating it as proof of a plan turns a description into an accusation.
Foot-in-the-Door.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Sunk Cost Exploitation points at what you have already invested to stop you from leaving; foot-in-the-door points at a past yes to win a new yes. Ultimatums force an either-or under threat of loss, while here nothing is threatened and the first agreement carries the weight. Urgency Manufacturing squeezes the clock, whereas the lever in this tactic is your own earlier consent, however unhurried the asking.

Urgency Manufacturing.short_definition: Pressing for an immediate decision, often by creating or inflating a deadline or emergency, so there is no time to think or ask anyone.
Urgency Manufacturing.core_meaning: Pressing for an immediate decision, often by creating or inflating a deadline or emergency, so there is no time to think or ask anyone.
Urgency Manufacturing.expanded_definition: Urgency manufacturing shrinks the time you have to decide, using a deadline or an emergency that may be invented or blown up from something small. Crisis Manufacturing is just another name for it, so a reader who knows it that way is in the right place. Real deadlines exist, so one rushed request tells you little. The pattern is a clock that appears whenever you want to think, check or consult someone, and when asking for time raises the pressure.
Urgency Manufacturing.plain_language_summary: You are told you must decide this minute, and asking for time to think only makes the pressure worse.
Urgency Manufacturing.why_this_matters: Without time you cannot compare, check facts or ask anyone you trust. A yes given under that squeeze is hard to take back, and afterwards you may feel foolish for agreeing to something you would have turned down on a calm day.
what_it_is: A time limit, real or inflated, placed on a decision that could wait.
Sometimes a whole emergency, such as a crisis only you can fix right now, built from something small through tone and framing.
Works by removing the chance to sleep on it, read the fine print or phone someone.
Seen in sales, scams, workplaces, families and relationships, from last-chance offers to late-night talks that must be settled now.
Usually stated by one side only, in a form you cannot easily check.
what_it_sounds_like: You have to decide right now.
This offer is gone by tonight.
There's no time to think about it. Just sign.
If you call anyone, it will be too late.
It's an emergency and only you can fix it, so I need you to act this minute.
Everyone else has already agreed. We're only waiting on you.
Answer me now. I can't wait until tomorrow.
A countdown timer on a checkout page that starts over when you reload it.
what_it_is_not: Real deadlines exist, such as a sale end date or a flight boarding time. Ask what actually happens if you take one more day.
Real emergencies feel exactly like this from the inside, and a burst pipe does need a call now.
Someone anxious who voices urgency because they feel it, with no view about how you decide.
An honest request for an answer by Friday because the venue needs a headcount, with the reason given.
Excitement, such as 'I'd love to do this soon', with nothing lost by waiting.
Time pressure from a process you both face, like an exam or an application window.
this_may_be_it_when: The deadline arrives just as you start asking questions or reaching for advice.
The deadline moves or comes back after it passes, as in 'okay, extended, but only until tomorrow'.
You are told not to consult anyone, or that consulting will ruin things.
The emergency cannot be confirmed by anyone except the person raising it.
Similar emergencies recur across unrelated matters, each needing an instant answer.
this_may_not_be_it_when: A reason for the deadline is given and a third party can confirm it.
Asking for a day brings a reply like 'sure, let me check whether that works'.
The deadline stays where it was after you ask about it.
Missing it costs something small and stated, and nobody leans on you.
The person who feels the rush is scrambling too and invites your help in thinking.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: People under real stress often speak fast and urgently without noticing the effect.
Businesses set real sale and booking cut-offs because of stock and capacity.
Someone with a deadline of their own may pass it along without realizing it feels like a squeeze.
common_false_positives: A genuine medical situation in which a decision does need to be made within the hour.
A landlord's deadline to return a lease that appears in the written terms.
A friend frantic over a lost passport before a flight, asking for a quick lift.
discernment_questions: Is there a reason for this deadline that I can check with someone other than the person pressing me?
What actually happens if I take one more day?
Does asking for time bring patience, or more pressure?
Has this deadline moved before, with no consequences?
Would I decide the same way on a calm morning?
less_concerning_if: The deadline comes from something outside the person and can be verified.
Time to think is granted without fuss when you ask.
The person states the cost of waiting plainly and leaves the choice to you.
more_concerning_if: You are told not to talk to anyone, or the people you would ask are described as not understanding.
The decision involves money, signing papers, sexual contact or giving up access to something you rely on.
Declining the rush brings anger, sulking or a hint of being cut off from something you need.
pattern_over_time_signs: Emergencies seem to arrive whenever a decision is wanted, and ease once you agree.
You have learned to decide fast and worry later, and you regret several earlier choices.
Deadlines slip afterwards without comment, as if they had never been real.
You dread messages or calls that start with 'quick question'.
Urgency Manufacturing.repair_check: Look at whether a request for time is now met with time. A changed exchange sounds like 'take the night, and tell me what else you'd like to know'. An apology followed by another 'by tonight' next week has changed the wording and nothing else.
Urgency Manufacturing.boundary_respect_check: Ask for one night and watch the answer. Patience, or a real reason why it cannot wait, is a good sign. A bigger emergency, sulking, or being told you do not care points the other way.
Urgency Manufacturing.psychological_mechanism: Pressure on time tends to push people toward quick, gut-level decisions in place of slow weighing. Checking facts and asking others both take time, so removing the time can remove those safeguards. A sense of emergency can also shift attention onto avoiding blame for a delay, so the decision itself stops being the focus.
Urgency Manufacturing.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe agreeing in a rush, then a sinking feeling afterwards and a clear sense that they would have said no with a day to think. Some feel on edge whenever a message arrives, or begin to distrust their own decisions. Others feel shame at having fallen for it, which can make them slower to ask for help next time.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask for a reason you can check: 'What happens if I answer tomorrow? Who sets that deadline?'
response_options.firm_boundary: State your pace: 'I don't make decisions like this on the spot. You'll have my answer tomorrow.'
response_options.disengagement: Stop answering the pressure itself. End the call or close the page, take the time anyway, and check the claim with an independent source before you reply.
response_options.support_seeking: Phone someone you trust before agreeing, even if you are told not to. Saying the details out loud often shows whether the rush is real.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, ask for the request and its deadline in writing, with the name of who set it, and bring in a manager or contract reviewer before you sign anything.

Urgency Manufacturing.boundary_script: "I don't give answers on the spot to things like this. I'll look at it tonight and tell you tomorrow. If the offer really ends before then, I accept that."
Urgency Manufacturing.safety_note: Most of the time this is a pressure problem, not a danger sign. It changes when the rush involves sending money, signing over property or papers, sexual contact, or a threat about what happens if you wait. In those cases, stop and phone someone you trust, your bank or a legal aid service before doing anything that cannot be undone.
misuse_warning: Not every deadline is manufactured. Calling a real, checkable deadline pressure can lead you to miss things that matter.
Telling a frightened or frantic person that they are manufacturing a crisis dismisses real distress and says more about what you assume than what you know.
Urgency Manufacturing.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Ultimatums force an either-or with a loss attached; urgency squeezes the clock and may leave several options open. False Dilemma narrows the options to two, where urgency only shortens the time to weigh whatever there is. Response-Time Policing objects after the fact that you were slow to reply, while this demands the answer before any delay can happen.

Frame Control.short_definition: Deciding what a conversation is about, through loaded labels or topic swaps, so that your actual concern has no place to land.
Frame Control.core_meaning: Deciding what a conversation is about, through loaded labels or topic swaps, so that your actual concern has no place to land.
Frame Control.expanded_definition: Frame control sets the terms of an exchange: what it is about, what is at stake and who plays which part. It covers more than one move. False Framing is another name for it, when a loaded label or extreme comparison settles the verdict before the facts arrive. Frame Assassination is a third name for it, when your point about an action is answered by turning the talk to your mood or character. One topic change in a tense talk is ordinary. The pattern is a frame that no version of your concern can fit inside.
Frame Control.plain_language_summary: The conversation keeps getting redefined as being about something else, often about you, so what you actually wanted to say never gets answered.
Frame Control.why_this_matters: An accurate account can come out sounding irrelevant, because the terms were set to leave it out before you spoke. You arrive with a concern about something that happened and leave defending your mood or motives, with your original point never refused and never answered.
what_it_is: Redefining the topic, the stakes or the roles so that your concern no longer matches the conversation.
Opening with a loaded label or an extreme comparison, so the verdict is settled before the facts are laid out.
Swapping a concern about an action for a remark about your tone, mood, character or history.
Persistent: restating your point sends it back into the same frame.
Can happen in writing, in meetings, in family disputes and in public statements, anywhere one account is allowed to name the subject.
what_it_sounds_like: This isn't about the dishes. This is about how unstable you've been lately.
We're not talking about what I said, we're talking about the way you took it.
Let's be honest, this is basically abandonment.
Do you hear yourself? That's the real issue here.
I think what you need to ask yourself is why this bothers you so much.
So now I'm the kind of person who would cheat. Is that what you think of me?
Your email asks about the missed payment, and the reply is two paragraphs on how hostile your tone was, with nothing on the payment.
what_it_is_not: Disagreeing in good faith about what the real issue is happens constantly, and both readings can have merit.
Steering a drifting talk back on topic together.
Someone raising a real worry about your wellbeing without meaning to displace what you said, who then returns to your point.
Describing a hurt in strong words because that is how it felt.
Choosing emphasis in an open argument, which is part of ordinary persuasion.
Agreeing to pause a heated talk and come back, with a time named and kept.
this_may_be_it_when: Your complaint names an action and the reply names a trait.
You can state your point three times and each time end up back at the new topic.
A label is attached to the situation before anyone has described what happened.
The conversation ends with you apologizing for how you raised it.
Days later, the original issue has no answer and nobody has mentioned it.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Your original point gets an answer, even a disagreeing one, before anything else is raised.
They ask 'can I say how this feels to me first?' and then return to your issue.
The concern about you is specific, such as that you have been sleeping badly, and they stay on your topic too.
The strong label still holds when the facts are listed plainly.
A time to resume is named and kept.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Some people go straight to their feelings when they feel attacked, and hear a complaint as a verdict on them.
In a long, tense talk both people lose the thread, and the topic changes without anyone choosing it.
People describe a hurt in dramatic words because that is how it felt, without meaning to settle the case in advance.
common_false_positives: A friend who says 'let's park this, I'm too tired to do it justice' and brings it back the next day.
A counselor who asks what else is going on for you, as part of an agreed session.
A partner who answers your complaint and also adds their own, so two topics now share the table.
discernment_questions: Can I still find my original point anywhere in this conversation?
When I restate it, does it get answered, or is it sent back to the new topic?
If I list only the facts, without the label, does the same conclusion follow?
Is the new subject one they would also raise on a calm day, with no complaint from me?
Would someone listening in say my concern was ever answered?
less_concerning_if: Your point gets at least a short answer before the talk widens.
The subject changes only when both of you are worn out, and returns when you are rested.
A strong label, once checked against the facts, turns out to hold.
more_concerning_if: The substitute topic is nearly always your character, mood or mental state.
You have stopped raising concerns because you know how they will end.
Other people are told the argument was about your reaction, not about the thing that set it off.
pattern_over_time_signs: You open complaints with long disclaimers about your tone, hoping to prevent the swap.
You find old concerns unanswered, with no memory of them being settled.
You say 'never mind' to end the talk, though the issue is unchanged.
Over months you bring up fewer concerns, and the list you keep in your head gets longer.
Frame Control.repair_check: Once you point out the swap, a changed exchange looks like them stating your original point back to you and answering it, even if the answer is no. An apology about the argument that never touches the original issue leaves that issue where it was.
Frame Control.boundary_respect_check: Notice whether you can hold your topic. Say once, 'I'd like an answer to my first question,' and see if it gets one. If the reply is more about you, the request was met with the very move it was about.
Frame Control.psychological_mechanism: Conversations follow whichever topic is emotionally louder. A remark about your stability or character is hard to ignore, so your effort moves to defending yourself, which is more tiring than complaining. A loaded label does similar work early, since later facts tend to be read through it. Pushing back on a personal remark can sound like proving it, and the original concern gets quietly dropped.
Frame Control.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe leaving a talk unable to say what they had meant to ask, replaying it for hours, and wondering whether they really are as difficult as they were just told. Some begin rehearsing complaints in advance, or stop raising them. A slow sense that nothing they bring up ever gets settled is also common.

response_options.soft_clarification: Name the swap and ask for both topics: 'I'd like to hear how I come across, and I'd also like an answer to what I first asked. Can we do mine first?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Hold your topic: 'That may be worth talking about, but it's not the subject today. I asked about the cancelled plans.'
response_options.disengagement: If the new topic keeps winning, stop the exchange and put the original concern in a short written note you can point back to.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend your original question and ask them to say back what they hear. If they can state it clearly, you know the question was not the problem.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work, put the concern in an email naming the action and the date, and ask for a reply on that point. A written thread keeps the topic from drifting.

Frame Control.boundary_script: "I notice we've moved from what I asked to how I'm asking. Could you tell me in one sentence what you make of the cancelled plans? Then I'll gladly hear what's on your mind."
Frame Control.safety_note: A conversation where someone else sets the terms is a conversation problem, not a danger sign. The picture changes if raising a concern starts to bring threats, punishments, or talk of your mental state to doctors or relatives. If that happens, note what was said and when, and talk to a counselor or advocate you trust before the next conversation about it.
misuse_warning: Calling it frame control whenever a talk changes topic punishes ordinary drift and hides the times you changed the subject yourself.
Used as an accusation, 'you're controlling the frame' can itself replace the other person's concern, which is the move it describes.
Frame Control.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Deflection steps away from the issue with a tangent or a counter-question, and often leaves the original frame standing; frame control replaces the frame itself, usually with you at the centre. Projection hands your complaint back as an accusation of the same behavior, while this hands it back as a remark about who you are. Priming / Narrative Seeding installs a lens before a talk begins, whereas this works inside the talk, as it unfolds.
